Fine gold content of all new jewellery (i.e. does not include exchanged

movements.

Medals and Imitation Coins.

1.1 Introduction
With gold having posted a new record nominal high 
of $1,679.50 at the time of writing, the yellow metal 
has reported a notable gain of almost $150 since the 
release of our last 3-Year Gold Forecast (on 27th May 
2011).  This impressive rally has largely reﬂected 
increasing concerns over sovereign debt problems in 
both Europe and the United States and the consequent 
damage to conﬁdence in most major currencies.  
The rally in the price from early July is all the more 
dramatic as it followed a relatively lacklustre few 
months for investment, as evidenced by the small 
growth in gold ETF holdings, limited interest in physical 
gold in Europe and some heavy liquidations of long 
positions on Comex.  Nonetheless, overall investment 
remained ﬁrmly in positive territory (World Investment 
showed a net inﬂow of $33 billion in the ﬁrst half of this 
year in total), thanks in part to good OTC buying and 
strong bar investment across Asia.  This reﬂects the 
ongoing importance of other factors such as heightened 
inﬂation concerns and low interest rates.  
Gold prices this year have also been supported by 
some favourable fundamental developments.  First 
and foremost, central banks have continued to add to 
their gold holdings in order to diversify ofﬁcial reserves 
away from the US dollar.  After an unexpected purchase 
of some 100 tonnes by Mexico early this year, Korea 
recently conﬁrmed that it bought 25 tonnes in June 
and July (its ﬁrst purchase in 13 years).  Basis GFMS 
statistics, net ofﬁcial sector purchases in the ﬁrst half 
of 2011 have already totalled more than 190 tonnes, 
against 73 tonnes over the same period last year.  In 
addition, scrap supply has remained moderate, with 
a limited response when the gold price breached 
$1,600 due to such factors as price accustomisation, 
stock depletion and bullish price expectations.  Lastly, 
jewellery fabrication has proved surprisingly robust 
(chieﬂy in India and China), with buying linked to this 
area particularly strong on any dip in the gold price.
Looking ahead, the fact that the gap between gold’s 
low and high so far this year stands at over $360 and 
the sudden scale of recent gains have all made for a 
challenging environment in which to forecast prices for 
the 2011-2013 period.  We had, for instance, expected 
a seasonal lull in demand and a bout of proﬁt taking to

produce a fairly signiﬁcant correction in gold prices over 
the summer but this is now looking unlikely.  
A key reason for this is the intrusion into the economic 
realm of politics (arguably a far trickier area to predict) 
by means of the worsening sovereign debt crisis in both 
Europe and the United States and it seems far from 
likely that political overspill has run its course.  Indeed, 
although US leaders have already given ﬁnal approval 
to legislation raising the country’s debt limit, the deal 
seems to be insufﬁcient to quell longer term disquiet; 
ﬁnancial markets now seem to be focusing on the 
growing prospect of a downgrade to the United States’ 
AAA credit rating as a credible policy to reduce the 
deﬁcit seems distant, particularly with a background 
of recent poor economic news.  In the Eurozone, 
peripheral yield spreads have also widened further, 
especially in Italian and Spanish bonds, which can be at 
least partially attributed to the reluctance of leaders at 
both a local and regional level to take painful decisions. 
To an extent, the eruption of this crisis has raised the 
prices in our Base Case towards levels once reserved 
for our most bullish variant, Scenario B.  This largely 
explains why we have trimmed the probability of this 
outcome from 50% at the time of our May report 
to 45% now.  All of this raises the possibility of a 
successful challenge of the $1,700 mark.  However, 
we think there remains a good chance that the rally 
in gold will lose momentum in coming weeks and that 
prices could consequently drop through hefty proﬁt

In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two 
alternative scenarios for the global economy that are 
very different to our central forecast.  In each instance, 
these have distinct implications for the level and 
trajectory of gold prices over the next three years.
  
Scenario B presents the most positive outlook for 
gold prices, with an investor led bull market continuing 
throughout the forecast period.  It is important to stress 
that we have raised the probability of this scenario 
from 30% to 40% since the previous report, reﬂecting 
the rapid deteriorating sovereign debt situation on 
both sides of the Atlantic.  A key difference between 
Scenario B and the Base Case is that the former 
assumes the persistence of sovereign debt problems for 
the next couple of years, rather than seeing the start 
of resolution next year.  As a consequence of this for 
example, we would be highly likely to see the United 
States’ credit rating downgraded in the short to medium 
term.  In addition, with weakness persisting in the US 
economy, we would expect the Fed to start a further 
round of monetary easing and maintain interest rates at 
ultra-low levels over almost the entire forecast period.  
Under such circumstances, a more rapid increase in 
inﬂation rates seems to be inevitable, particularly in 
the United States where the CPI is forecast to rise to 
taking.  Nonetheless, it could well be that prices fail to 
penetrate far below $1,650 and the $1,600 mark looks 
out of reach.  The reasons for this are as follows.
Firstly as noted earlier, although immediate sovereign 
debt worries may ease, problems are expected to re-
emerge again later.  Meanwhile, given the currently 
weak state of the US economy, the Federal Reserve 
is likely to keep interest rates unchanged for at least 
another 6-12 months, which will keep the dollar under 
pressure.  Another factor, that could well come into 
play is inﬂation expectations.  So far this year we 
have already seen that some investors are concerned 
at the prospect of future inﬂation, especially in the 
United States.  Such concerns could grow in future 
should there be indications that governments and 
central banks are prepared to maintain loose ﬁscal and 
monetary policies to stimulate economic growth.  
As such, under our Base Case, we expect to see further 
gains in investment demand later this year and for 
this to once again drive gold higher, generating a clear 
breach of the $1,700 mark by year-end.  For the full 
year, this would give us a fresh all-time nominal record 
of an annual average of $1,560 (a level notably higher 
than the $1,490 forecast in the May report).
Moving to 2012, we assume the above factors will 
continue to support gold investment, with the price 
trading above $1,600 for at least the ﬁrst few months 
of the year.  However, it may prove difﬁcult to sustain 
investment and therefore the price unless fresh, gold-
supportive news emerges.  This could therefore begin 
to threaten prices as we move further into the year, 
particularly if the global economy shows clear signs 
of having returned to stable growth and if central 
banks ﬁnd themselves obliged to begin a round of 
interest rate rises or in other ways unwind stimuli.  
Nonetheless, the retreat for investment could be 
fairly orderly given the reluctance of some monetary 
authorities to tighten policy, particularly in the United 
States.  Furthermore, the emergence of rising inﬂation 
(perhaps more a feature for 2013), particularly in the 
United States (where the CPI is forecast to reach 4.1% 
in 2013), will also help to limit the fall in gold prices. 
Even if we are not forecasting a rout in this scenario, 
we still expect a steady slide in prices to get underway 
in 2012 but, due to a higher starting point, the annual 
average could still rise year-on-year, with our current 
estimate standing at $1,565 (up notably from May’s 
$1,465).  However, even if the boom has proved bigger

our growing conﬁdence in producers’ ability to bring 
projects into production in a timely manner.  Despite a 
falling price in 2013, we still expect there to be enough 
momentum behind mine supply to push growth at that 
time, albeit at a much slower pace.  It is of note that 
our forecast has been revised upward modestly, mainly 
due the upward revision in our price forecast.  
In spite of a major increase in gold prices this year, 
scrap supply is forecast to rise by only a modest 
7%.  In part, this is because expectations of further 
price gains have seen many consumers hold back from 
selling.  Furthermore, there was a degree of depletion 
in near market stocks in some markets, with jewellery 
holdings already having been liquidated, typically 
during previous periods of high prices.  With gold 
entering a declining trend at some point during 2012, 
scrap supply will also start to retreat, although volumes 
still remain very high in 2013 by historical standards.   
Turning to demand, our forecast for jewellery is little 
changed since the previous forecast.  Speciﬁcally, 
demand is expected to increase by a small 2% in 2011, 
despite rising prices.  Nevertheless, it is important 
to note that almost all of this growth will come from 
India and China, as bullish price expectations, stable 
growth in incomes and rising inﬂation have generated 
very healthy demand in both countries so far this 
year.  Excluding the two, jewellery offtake is forecast to 
remain generally weak, a result of elevated prices plus 
sluggish economic growth in western countries.  While 
prices will drop considerably in the latter part of the 
forecast, demand will rise only modestly, with its total 
in 2013 still well below its pre-crisis level.  
Other fabrication is set to increase by 7% to 807 
tonnes in 2011, on the back of higher electronics and 
coin offtake.  Thereafter, while the former will continue 
to grow, the latter is forecast to decline, leaving the 
overall ﬁgure broadly ﬂat in both 2012 and 2013.  
Net ofﬁcial sector purchases are forecast to rise 
by more than 230 tonnes to 305 tonnes this year and 
then average 225 tonnes in 2012-2013.  Our forecast 
has been revised upward since the previous report, 
basis the latest announcement from Korea who bought 
25 tonnes in June and July coupled with ongoing 
robust purchases from a number of emerging market 
countries, including Thailand, Russia and Mexico, all of 
which have reported further increases in gold holdings 
in the second quarter of this year.  
5.5% by 2013.  Furthermore, it is very likely that the 
authorities will be tempted to tolerate a rise in inﬂation 
if this boosts GDP growth and reduces the real level of 
public debt.  In line with this, Scenario B also envisages 
a sharp drop in the value of the US dollar.  These 
factors should prompt a far broader move into gold 
among institutional investors, which in turn will result 
in gold prices advancing in each year of the forecast 
to an average of $2,090 in 2013.  That outcome is 
substantially higher than forecast in May, when the rally 
was expected to take us to $1,940 in that year.
A complete contrast is Scenario C, where investment 
will start to slip this year.  Given the greater likelihood 
of a continuation of loose ﬁscal and monetary policies 
in the United States, we assign this scenario a 15% 
probability, 5% lower than in May.  Under this scenario, 
the weakness in the gold price is basis a secular 
recovery in the dollar and a low level of inﬂation, 
reﬂecting governments’ failure to boost private demand 
and consumer spending in advanced economies.  The 
prolonged period of low inﬂation in western countries 
will also be compounded by further austerity measures 
and tighter monetary policy at a time when economic 
growth is still sluggish and unemployment rates remain 
high.  These factors should reduce gold’s appeal to 
investors, most notably from 2012 onwards, when 
a marked reduction in investment results in prices 
slipping to levels that are more in line with gold’s 
underlying supply/demand fundamentals.  
It is of note that the gold price under this scenario has 
been revised upward noticeably compared with our 
previous forecast.  This reﬂects the recent pick up in 
investor interest and a higher likely starting point for 
the gold price in forthcoming years.
Much of the above has focused on the principal 
economic variables and investment.  As mentioned 
previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view 
that price direction and level are determined by 
investment alone.  The following analysis of expected 
trends in the underlying supply/demand variables 
shows that these will also play an important, if 
subsidiary, role in gold price determination in 2011-13.
1.2 The Base Case Scenario

to continue rising throughout the forecast period as 
it posts successive records and reaches a peak of 
2,957 tonnes in 2013.  This forecast is premised on an

Implied net investment is forecast to drop by some 
90 tonnes this year.  Despite a fall, however, the 2011 
ﬁgure is still well above the long term average of 
some 230 tonnes in 2000-08.  Key drivers behind this 
elevated investment demand are continued sovereign 
debt fears, very loose monetary policies in western 
countries and rising inﬂation fears, all of which are 
expected to remain in place over much of 2012.  Our 
implied ﬁgure therefore will post a modest recovery 
next year before a major fall of nearly 30% takes place 
in 2013.  The series has been marked higher since the 
May, reﬂecting increasing investor interest in response 
to the worsening sovereign debt situation in both 
Europe and the United States.  
Bar investment is expected to rise by some 100 
tonnes to a new record level in 2011.  While investment 
in western countries will be mainly driven by ongoing 
uncertainties regarding the debt problem as well as 
continued low interest rates, demand in key Asian 
markets will be largely underpinned by very bullish 
price expectations and safe haven purchases against 
rising inﬂation (particularly in China).  Even though the 
investment case for gold will start to wane in 2013, 
demand is likely to maintain rather solid, which should 
provide great support for the gold price in that year.  
Finally, net producer de-hedging will remain subdued 
in both 2011 and 2012, given the limited size of the 
outstanding hedgebook as well as the fact that many 
of the contracts on the book are project hedges.  As 
the price begins to fall towards the end of the forecast 
period, we expect a return to net hedging by producers 
to lock in favourable prices.  However, given the mining 
industry’s current innate bias against hedging, we do 
not anticipate this to be widespread.

1.3 Scenario B
Scenario B features GFMS’ most positive assessment 
of gold prices, which are forecast to continue rising 
to a new record high of $2,090 (basis the annual 
average) in 2013.  This performance will be almost 
entirely due to a marked rise in global investment 
demand in response largely to the growing inﬂationary 
environment and sovereign debt crisis.  This pushes the 
global total for investment to successive new record 
highs from 2011 to 2013, in both volume and value 
terms.  By 2013, investment demand is forecast to 
amount to 3,363 tonnes, or almost 1,500 tonnes higher 
than 2011’s already record position.  The performance 
in value terms will be even more acute, with the total 
expected to more than double between 2011 and 
2013.  This further highlights the overriding importance 
of investment demand to the price outcome over this 
period.  For example, during 2001-10 investment 
demand averaged $21 billion, compared with a forecast 
average (over the next three years) of $158 billion.  
In contrast, jewellery consumption is set to fall heavily  
to below 1,600 tonnes by 2013.  This outcome, which 
is overwhelmingly due to the impact of higher prices, 
highlights one of the key differences with the Base Case 
supply/demand balance, with jewellery consumption 
here some 570 tonnes lower than under the Base Case.
As for supply, mine production posts successive and 
partially price-led notable gains to over 3,000 tonnes 
by 2013 but scrap posts a yet more robust response 
to higher prices, with recycling expected to approach 
2,500 tonnes by the end of the forecast.  As a result, 
by 2013 scrap will account for around 44% of global 
supply under Scenario B, compared with a less heady  
but still signiﬁcant 32% under the Base Case.

2.2 Economic Backdrop
Since our last report, concerns over the debt problem 
in both Europe and the United States have taken centre 
stage as the immediate consequences of the Japanese 
earthquake for ﬁnancial markets began to subside.  
Starting with the former, a year after European 
governments and the IMF had lent Greece €110 billion 
to lighten its debt burden, Portugal became the third 
eurozone member to accept ﬁnancial assistance in 
May before the EU and IMF agreed a second bailout to 
Greece worth €159 billion.  Indeed, the scale of this 
crisis is such that it threatens to spread to some of 
Europe’s biggest economies such as Spain and Italy.  
2.1 Introduction
GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented 
in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, 
namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and 
Scenario C.  Under our Base Case, we expect a 
slowdown in global GDP growth this year, partly as the 
effect of ﬁscal stimulus plans ebb or austerity measures 
begin to bite, before a gradual pick up in growth 
occurs over the ﬁnal two years of our forecast due to 
improvements in the underlying world economy.  We 
view this as the most likely scenario, but the probability 
of our Base Case has been lowered slightly by 5% to 
45% since our May forecast.  
Our more bullish Scenario B, to which we assign a 
40% probability, predicts inﬂation rising over the next 
three years, albeit modestly at ﬁrst, above all in the 
United States.  Central to this scenario are the policies 
being followed by the US government and the Federal 
Reserve, including a continuation of the very loose 
ﬁscal and monetary policy.  Such policies are forecast to 
largely avert a renewed economic slowdown in 2011-
13 but at the cost of rising inﬂation, with it reaching 
an annual average of 5.5% in 2013.  Moreover, the US 
dollar weakens under this scenario.  It is of note that 
we have raised the possibility of Scenario B by 10% 
since our May forecast, reﬂecting increasing concerns 
over the sovereign debt problem on both sides of the 
Atlantic over the last couple of months.

2.3 The Base Case Scenario
Our forecast for global economic growth in 2011 has 
been revised lower since our last report.  After a major 
rebound in 2010, world GDP growth is set to slow down 
this year to 2.7%, down slightly from 2.9% in our May 
forecast.  This is due to the indebted nature of both 
governments and consumers in much of the developed 
world.  Meanwhile, further tightening of monetary 
policies in emerging markets to ﬁght surging inﬂation 
will also slow down world GDP growth this year.  This 
is followed by marginally faster growth in 2012 and 
2013 as the more traditional sources of growth, such 
as consumer spending and the property market, start 
to improve.  The latter will be aided by unemployment 
beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels.  
US GDP grew at an annualised rate of 1.3% in the 
second quarter, well below market expectations.  
The main reason for the disappointing ﬁgure was 
weak consumer spending, as this key driver of the 
US economy rose by a mere 0.1% over the same 
period.  This reﬂects a continuation of an elevated 
unemployment rate coupled with a lacklustre property 
market, both of which are likely to remain in place for 
an extended period.  While the Fed could start further 
unconventional policies to stimulate the economy, ﬁscal 
room is becoming extremely limited.  Indeed, even 
though the debt ceiling deal has been passed by the 
US House of Representatives, investors’ concerns over 
the country’s debt problem will remain heightened in 
the medium-to-long term.  Furthermore, increasing 
inﬂation pressure and requests for higher yield on 
its treasury bonds from developing countries will 
eventually see the Fed tighten its policy in late 2012.  
This combined with the waning support from ﬁscal 
policy will certainly restrict annual GDP growth to 
around 2% in the ﬁnal two years of the forecast.  
Despite renewed concerns over the sovereign debt 
problem, the recovery in EU-27 has been gaining 
traction, although intra-European growth differentials 
are set to widen.  Germany, for example, grew 1.5% 
in the ﬁrst quarter, lifting activity in Europe’s largest 
economy back over the previous 2008 peak.  In 
contrast, growth in Italy and Spain remained sluggish, 
with Portugal falling back into recession over the 
same period.  Key to this are the lingering impact of 
the sovereign debt crisis and the accelerating ﬁscal 
adjustment.  Looking ahead, growth in the southern 
European countries is projected to lag growth in the 
euro area’s larger economies.  Therefore, average 
EU growth will be around 1.3% in 2011.  Given the 
excessive levels of public debt in many European 
countries, we would envisage austerity measures 
continue throughout the forecast.  As such, we continue 
to expect only modest GDP growth in 2012 and 2013 in 
this region as its economies gradually recover.

many countries where inﬂation has already picked up

In contrast, the latest comment from Bernake indicated 
that the Federal Reserve is ready to start QE3 if the 
economy continues to worsen.  In fact, until there is 
credible evidence that the Fed is likely to raise interest 
rates in the near term, the dollar is likely to remain 
under pressure.  As such, we expect the dollar:euro 
rate to rise to an average of $1.40/€ this year.  
Nevertheless, mainly based on its current purchasing

US dollar to strengthen against the euro in the latter

Besides the convergence towards long run PPP referred

by then the Federal Reserve will, ﬁnally, start to raise 
interest rates from their current exceptionally low 
levels.  We therefore expect the US dollar to average 
$1.38/€ in 2012 and $1.35/€ in 2013.

2.5 Scenario C

advanced economies border on very low levels of 
inﬂation.  Therefore, global GDP growth is a poor

single economy, the United States, where, as a result,

1.2% in 2012, before a slight improvement in 2013.  
In Europe, the outlook also looks bleak as economic

2.6 Gold Price Scenarios
The 2011 annual average price forecast for the Base 
Case scenario has been revised higher since the 
previous report by $40 to $1,560.  This is mainly 
driven by recent buoyant investor interest, although 
growing support for the price from gold’s underlying 
fundamentals is also important to the outcome.  For 
example, despite higher gold prices seen in the second 
quarter, jewellery demand remained robust while scrap 
supply moderated.  
Looking at the rest of the year, we remain generally 
bullish over the gold price, although a small decline in 
prices is likely to take place if the current momentum 
runs out of steam.  However, it is important to point 
out that any correction in price will prove short-lived as 
the prospect of a softer US dollar in 2011 and concerns 
over the sustainability of the country’s government 
debt will stoke further investment interest in the 
gold market.  In addition to the stimulus this should 
provide for gold investment this year, there is also the 
probability of a continued debasement of ﬁat currencies 
as other economies may follow the United States down 
this path in an attempt to stimulate their economies.  
Consequently, gold will rally to a series of fresh record 
highs later this year, with the price expected to trade 
well above $1,700 before year-end.  
Given that monetary policies across western countries 
are likely to remain loose at least through to the ﬁrst 
half of next year, investment is set to stay robust in 
2012.  However, signs of the end of the bull run should 
start to emerge before the end of that year, not least 
as the US dollar will have begun to appreciate on a 
secular basis, in no small measure due to the Federal 
Reserve raising interest rates in response to inﬂationary 
pressures.  As a result, gold is forecast to start 
declining in 2012 but, given the high starting price, the 
annual average will still rise slightly, to $1,565.  Against 
this backdrop, investment demand then weakens, with 
the gold price subsequently declining to an annual 
average of $1,340 in 2013.
Our most bullish gold price outlook is encapsulated in 
Scenario B.  This sees US inﬂation rising throughout 
the forecast period to reach 5.5% in 2013 on the 
back of further quantitative easing by the Fed.  Given 
that the US government is reluctant to cut its debt 
level, this scenario also assumes that concerns over 
the sovereign debt problem in all major industrialised 
countries will continue to grow, with the United States 
very likely to lose its ‘AAA’ credit rating.  As such, we 
expect sustained weakness in the US dollar, dropping 
to an annual average low for the forecast period of 
$1.57/€ in 2013.  This presents a highly favourable 
environment for gold investment, which is projected 
to increase in tonnage and especially in value terms 
each year over 2011-13.  This has led us to raise our 
forecast for the 2011 average since the May report to 
$1,575, while our forecasts for 2012 and 2013 have 
respectively been upped to $1,835 and $2,090.  It 
should be noted that, in the latter year our World 
Investment category exceeds 3,000 tonnes for the ﬁrst 
time, comfortably outstripping global mine production.
Scenario C is our more bearish outlook for prices, in 
which they are expected to follow a downward path 
during the forecast.  The outlook is based on the 
assumption that there is a strong rebound in the dollar, 
especially against the euro as the focus switches from 
the travails of the US economy back to the troubled 
economies of Europe.  However, this year investment 
will be supported by fears of an economic slowdown in 
many advanced economies, which has therefore seen 
gold prices stay close to record levels over the rest of 
the year.  As a result, average annual gold prices in 
2011 should still reach a nominal record of $1,500.  
Nevertheless, in 2012 and 2013 the downtrend in 
prices intensiﬁes, predicated on declining investment 
demand due to further austerity measures taken by 
governments in major countries to ﬁght surging debt, 
inﬂation staying very low and, eventually, interest rates 
rising.  Indeed, in 2013 the implied net investment 
total is at its lowest level on an annual basis since 
disinvestment occurred in 2004.  As a result, gold 
prices weaken, although the decline is moderated by 
a major improvement in jewellery demand.  The net 
result is that gold averages $1,385 in 2012 and $1,130 
in 2013.  These prices have also been revised upwards 
since our last report due mainly to the higher ‘starting 
price’ in 2011 than previously forecast.

3.1 Mine Production
Since the last report, GFMS have adjusted the gold 
price outlook upwards for each scenario, with the most 
notable changes to the alternative scenarios, B and C.  
Consequently, we have increased forecast mine supply 
volumes under all three scenarios, but there are 
constraining factors which will, we believe, reduce 
the divergence in production volumes between the 
scenarios.  
To a large extent, production in 2011 and 2012 will be 
governed by an existing pipeline of projects currently 
under construction.  The chart below plots this 
potential production, using data from GFMS’ proprietary 
database of mines, aggregated by probability of timely 
start up, as judged by GFMS.  This partially subjective 
judgement is based on criteria such as project quality, 
development stage, company track record and funding.  
There will inevitably be instances of underperformance 
at some operations, and delays or setbacks to 
production schedules, for a multitude of reasons, some 
exogenous and beyond the control of the developer.  
Hence actual volumes of global mine supply always 
tend to fall below the maximum level implied by miners’ 
plans; under each of our scenarios, we take a slightly 
different view on the degree to which production 
delays and upsets will negatively impact upon potential 
production.  
Besides developments in the larger-scale formal mining 
sector, we must also consider small-scale and alluvial 
production, including more operating environments 
such as China, which tend to be more opaque to 
analysis. These production sources are typically more 
responsive to gold price changes, and are therefore 
forecast to react differently under our alternate 
economic outlooks.  
Forecasting output at the tail end of the forecast period 
is inherently more speculative; under all three scenarios 
2013 sees the largest increase in our forecast numbers 
relative to the last edition of this forecast.

3.1.2 Scenario B
This scenario sees the strongest rise in mine supply,

restriction being the pipeline of projects currently 
under development.  Under scenario B, growth in mine 
supply will, however, come from several additional 
sources compared with the other scenarios.  Firstly, we 
believe a strongly increasing gold price will encourage 
additional output from the small-scale and artisanal 
mining sector.  Secondly, gold companies will look to 
re-evaluate projects and redesign operating parameters 
to maximise potential asset value due to the rising 
price environment.  As a result miners will carry 
out additional feasibility work to study throughput 
expansions, incorporate additional satellite deposits in 
their production schedules etc.  Mine life extensions 
will occur at many operations where a higher price will 
allow reserve calculations to be revised.  
Under this scenario we also expect there to be fewer

forecast under the Base Case, while at the other end of 
the scale existing operations will see expanding margins 
alleviating potential cost pressures, allowing them to 
produce more higher-cost ounces.  
3.1.2 Scenario C
Under this scenario we expect the a declining gold 
price trend to slow the pace of growth in mine 
production.  This is based on a view that ongoing plans 
for expansions may be put on hold, or at least watered 
down somewhat given falling prices.  Furthermore, 
falling prices will lower the possibility of producers 
expanding reserve bases by increasing the gold prices 
used in economic feasibility studies.  While this will not 
actively reduce mine supply at the price levels forecast, 
it will certainly act to limit the extent of potential 
production upside at many properties.   
Therefore, relative to our previous forecast, we have 
not increased our Scenario C mine production forecasts

miners will also begin to experience appreciable margin 
pressure, with real gold prices falling below $1,000/

scenario there will be a reduction in output from the

4.1 Introduction
Scrap has been on a rising trend for the last decade or 
so, roughly tripling from around 600 tonnes a year in 
the mid-1990s to a record 1,690 tonnes in 2009.  Over 
the longer term, one has to consider the rising pool of 
potential jewellery scrap, but recent growth has had far 
more to do with rising gold prices (often inﬂated further 
locally by currency weakness) and ﬁnancial turmoil, 
which triggered notable distress selling.
Despite higher prices, 2010 deviated slightly from trend 
as some held back from selling, expecting further price 
gains.  These withheld supplies should emerge this year 
which, together with other price-led selling, should see 
a fresh record for scrap.  Under our Base Case, the 
start of a secular price slide at some point during 2012, 
an improvement in the speed and solidity of world GDP 
growth and signs that much of the loosely held material 
in the industrialised world has already been sold means 
a slight dip in total scrap next year.  A much steeper fall 
then occurs in 2013 as the above forces intensify.
Scenario C’s scrap also sees a rise, if more modest, 
in 2011 and again losses in 2012 and 2013, with the 
latter year hitting a six-year low.  Much of this retreat 
will be driven by the price fall, although the eventual 
improvement in the macroeconomic backdrop and 
low near-market industrialised world stocks will also 
contribute.  Scenario B also sees a fresh record in 2011 
but, in contrast, its still rising price means further highs 
are set in 2012 and 2013.  Implicit in this forecast is a 
belief that near-market stocks in the developing world 
are sufﬁcient to feed ever-rising scrap and compensate 
for depleted industrialised world supplies.  
Changes to scrap since May include a narrowing of the 
spread between scenarios for 2011 as we are over half 
way through the year.  This mainly entailed a major 
lift for Scenario C and a fair cut for Scenario B.  The 
2012 forecast for Scenario C and yet more so the Base 
Case have also been raised due to higher prices but 
2013 is little changed, on the assumption that a greater 
share of loosely held material would have already been 
sold.  Another factor behind the cut in Scenario B’s 
2011 scrap is slower than anticipated Middle East ﬂows 
and this lower starting point plus the fact that price 
revisions are less radical means the 2012 and 2013 
scrap estimates are slightly reduced.
4.2 Industrialised World
In that the industrialised world’s scrap in 2010 rose 
by not far off a ﬁfth, it behaved very differently to the 
developing world whose scrap fell by around 10%.  The 
former group’s rise was partly due to high gold prices 
as these helped fund heavy advertising by collectors 
but perhaps of equal importance were growing 
consumer awareness of increasingly attractive recycling 
possibilities, a drop in the stigma attached to selling 
back and high unemployment in some countries.
The key feature of our 2011 Base Case industrialised 
world estimate is that it is hardly different to the 2010 
result.  This is chieﬂy down to the depletion of near 
market stocks proving strong enough to counter both 
higher prices and a deterioration in the economic 
outlook for several countries.  Indeed, this year 
already shows a split within this grouping as scrap 
from southern Europe, Japan and the United States 
is proving more buoyant in comparison respectively 
with northern Europe, Canada and elsewhere in 
industrialised Asia.  The estimates for both Scenario B 
and C are also little changed on 2010 as the former’s 
scrap is boosted by far higher prices and the latter’s 
by greater distress selling.  Both the Base Case and 
Scenario C then see steady losses in 2012 and 2013 
due to falling gold prices and economic improvement, 
taking both 2013 estimates to ﬁve-year lows.  In 
contrast, Scenario B’s scrap rises in both 2012 and 
2013, with hefty trade destocking a possibility.  
However, overall gains are slight due to consumer stock 
depletion and a swifter exit from economic malaise.
Changes since the last report essentially comprise 
modest increases in all scenarios in most years.  
This reﬂects both higher forecast prices and the 
deterioration in economic prospects for several 
countries, particularly in southern Europe.

Global Scrap Supply
4.3 Developing World
The developing world has witnessed a material increase 
in scrap supply over the last decade, peaking at record 
levels in 2009, as gold prices rallied.  Scrap supply from 
this bloc of countries fell in 2010 despite the 26% rise 
in the average dollar gold price, with this unexpected 
change in trend due to a number of motivating factors.  
Firstly, consumers in several markets had become 
accustomed to the new, higher price level, particularly 
in an environment of lower price volatility and were 
therefore often reluctant to liquidate gold assets with 
expectations of yet higher prices to prevail.  Secondly, 
weakness in the US dollar meant that in many cases 
the gold price in domestic currency terms failed to 
register quite the same percentage gains as did dollar 
prices.  Finally, there was a degree of near-market 
depletion in several countries, with signiﬁcant gold 
assets already liquidated, often during previous periods 
of buoyant prices. 
A key characteristic of most of these price sensitive 
markets remains the dominance of low labour cost and 
high carat jewellery.  Indeed, this low margin structure 
is the major reason why gold jewellery can often be 
viewed as quasi-investment vehicle in these markets, 
with consumers willing to “invest” in plain jewellery 
with the clear intention of selling the item back should 
the gold price move higher and a proﬁt be obtained.
  
While these market characteristics remain broadly 
in place, there has been a slow but nevertheless 
noteworthy shift within traditional styles away from 
heavy plain designs to light weight items and an 
increase in the use of stones to lower the precious 
metal content.  Rising gold prices remain the chief 
catalyst for this transformation as manufacturers in 
the last few years have attempted to maintain retail 
price points to attract a declining consumer base.  
Nonetheless, we would be surprised if this trend were 
to completely reverse should prices begin a secular 
slide.  In addition, we have seen growth for more 
fashion focused high margin jewellery that is more 
‘western’ in style.  Both these trends are potentially 
signiﬁcant for scrap as lighter, gemset or branded 
pieces are less likely to be scrapped.  However, while 
these consumption trends are gaining momentum (from 
a very low base), the impact on scrap at this point 
remains slight and is unlikely to become inﬂuential 
within this three-year forecast period.
Looking to this year, and ﬁrstly at the Base Case, 
GFMS expect scrap supply from the developing world to 
respond to surging domestic gold prices, with healthy 
gains forecast for most markets in this grouping.  
However, on current expectations, it could still prove 
lower than the record high of 2009.  Following this near 
double-digit gain in 2011, we expect supply to ease 
modestly in 2012, before a more signiﬁcant fall of over 
15% is forecast for 2013 as the gold price slumps.  
Under Scenario C, a not dissimilar trajectory is 
forecast.  However, the decline in scrap supply over 
the ﬁnal two years is more pronounced as weaker gold 
prices prevail, retreating almost 15% in both 2012 and 
2013 respectively.  There is no such decline under the 
high price environment of Scenario B, with record 
prices delivering the opportunity for further increases; 
following a jump of over 20% this year, similar 
gains are expected in both 2012 and 2013, reaching 
successive record highs in these years.
Changes since the last report for the Base Case include 
a modest cut to the 2011 estimate, with the downward 
revision quite notable for the Middle East and India.  
This is chieﬂy due to slower than expected ﬂows so 
far this year due to greater withholding of supplies in 
anticipation of higher prices to come.  The emergence 
of these withheld volumes and higher forecast prices 
then mean an upward revision for the 2012 scrap ﬁgure 
but a slight cut in 2013 due to higher remelt of stocks 
in the prior year.  Slower ﬂows this year and less radical 
revisions to prices mean that scrap under Scenario B 
has in fact been trimmed since May in all three years.  
Part of the cut for 2011 reﬂects a narrowing of the 
spread across scenarios as we are now some way into 
the year.  This also shows in Scenario C, whose 2011 
scrap estimate has been raised signiﬁcantly.  Higher 
forecast prices in 2012 and 2013 have also fed through 
to greater scrap numbers, although higher earlier stock 
melt means these increases are not great.

5.1 Introduction
The ofﬁcial sector was a consistent net seller of gold 
on an annual basis from the end of the 1980s through 
to the end of the 2000s.  For instance, from 2000-
09 the ofﬁcial sector’s contribution to global supply 
averaged 443 tonnes per annum, with particularly 
heavy disposals, mainly by countries within the Central 
Bank Gold Agreement (CBGA), in 2003 and 2005.  
However, the pace of selling from the ofﬁcial sector 
slowed considerably in 2008 and then more so in 2009, 
when net sales fell to just 34 tonnes, their lowest level 
in more than two decades.  In addition, a sharp fall in 
releases from CBGA signatories, coupled with continued 
purchases outside the Agreement, actually resulted in 
the ofﬁcial sector in aggregate becoming a modest net 
purchaser on annual basis in 2010, a case last seen in 
1988.
5.2 Base Case
Looking ahead, consistent with the previous report, we 
expect a major increase in net ofﬁcial sector purchases 
this year.  While net purchases are forecast to fall from 
next year onward, their absolute levels will stay high 
by historical standards, with net buying amounting to 
200 tonnes by the end of the forecast.  Nevertheless, 
we have raised our ﬁgure for 2011 and 2012 by 45 and 
20 tonnes respectively since the May report, due to 
growing buy-side interest from a number of countries in 
this year.  
There are three main reasons why we believe net 
ofﬁcial sector purchases will increase sharply this year 
and remain fairly high thereafter.  First, the IMF, which 
accounted for 62% and 94% of overall gross sales in 
2009 and 2010 respectively, completed its gold sales 
programme in December 2010.  Meanwhile, sales 
from the CBGA signatories will remain at extremely 
low levels over the forecast period, as those that were 
inclined to sell have already substantially reduced their 
bullion stocks.  Furthermore, given persistent concerns 
over the sovereign debt crisis in the Eurozone, it is 
unlikely that there will be any major disposals from the 
group.  
Third, looking at countries outside the CBGA, already in 
the past two years we have seen this group become net 
buyers of gold.  Basis the latest IMF statistics, Mexico 
increased their gold reserves by almost 100 tonnes in 
the ﬁrst ﬁve months of 2011.  Meanwhile, Russia, the 
largest gold buyer last year, has continued their regular 
purchases this year.  Elsewhere, Thailand which bought 
nearly 16 tonnes in September 2010, also reported an 
increase of 27 tonnes so far this year.  Finally, in early 
August, the central bank Korea also conﬁrmed that 
it increased its gold reserves (for the ﬁrst time in 13 
years) by 25 tonnes in June and July. 
Moving forward there is scope for a similar level of gold 
purchases from the non-CBGA group, particularly by 
those countries with both signiﬁcant US dollar foreign 
exchange holdings as well as a low share of gold in 
their foreign reserves.

Even in the Eurozone, where the European Central Bank

As such, gold’s traditional ‘Achilles heel’ (the fact that it 
pays very little in the way of interest) should not be a

Besides these factors favouring buy-side activities, we 
should also mention a change in most central banks’ 
attitude towards gold from the highly negative extreme 
that it had reached in many cases over the 1990s 
and early 2000s during the extended bear market at 
that time.  Apart from the exogenous ﬁnancial factors 
referred to above, that have led to a reconsideration of 
gold’s properties as an inherently risk-free asset (unlike 
government debt and ﬁat currencies), this change in 
attitude stems from the yellow metal’s consistently 
positive price performance in most currencies over the 
last few years.
Nevertheless, although we expect the ofﬁcial sector 
to remain a net buyer over the next three years, it is 
important to note that large-scale, direct purchases 
from the major holders of foreign exchange reserves, 
such as China, in the open market appears unlikely.  
This is mainly due to the potential for such transactions 
to disrupt gold and foreign exchange markets and also, 
in some cases, for them to create political difﬁculties 
(for example, with the United States).  Furthermore, 
although price is not the key issue regarding an 
institution’s choice to augment its gold reserves, for 
some potential buyers this consideration may well affect 
the timing of any such purchases.  We would expect, 
instead, further discreet and modestly sized operations 
to be carried out in the international market, coupled 
with the purchase of local mine supply by certain 
countries where domestic mine production is available.  
Over time and in aggregate, however, such operations 
could account for a not insubstantial contribution to 
gold demand and therefore be supportive of gold prices.
  
5.3 Alternative Scenarios
As mentioned above, although ofﬁcial sector activity is 
largely policy-driven, the timing of sales and purchases 
can be inﬂuenced by price considerations.  Under 
Scenario C, lower gold prices would trigger more 
purchases over the forecast period, with the ofﬁcial 
sector as a whole reporting a slightly higher level of net 
purchases from 2011 to 2013 compared with the Base 
Case.  
In contrast, under Scenario B, due to the higher 
gold price environment, we expect that some of these 
potential purchases will be postponed, with net ofﬁcial 
sector purchases being limited to 280 tonnes this 
year before falling to 200 tonnes and 100 tonnes in 
2012 and 2013 respectively.  Another factor to bear 
in mind is that some central banks that trade part of 
their bullion reserves might take proﬁts on what are 
perceived to be temporary spikes in the gold price.
It is of note that as with Base Case, our forecast under 
both Scenario B and Scenario C has been raised since 
the previous report, reﬂecting very strong net ofﬁcial 
sector purchases seen so far this year.

four lines, namely physical bar investment, ofﬁcial

Investment, which is shown in the table opposite.  In 
2010, World Investment totalled 1,687 tonnes, down 
by 9% year-on-year.  It is worth stressing that, despite 
a small decline, last year’s ﬁgure was still the second 
highest in two decades and 178% higher than the 
average seen over the 2000-08 period.  
Looking ahead, forecasts for World Investment vary 
greatly under our different scenarios.  Under the Base 
Case, a small increase in investment is expected in 
both 2011 and 2012, driven mainly by the ongoing 
sovereign debt crisis, ultra-low interest rates and 
growing inﬂationary fears. Thereafter, investor interest 
in gold will start to falter, although its absolute level will 
remain even elevated by 2013.  For Scenario C, World 
Investment is forecast to drop slightly this year before 
a more substantial decline emerges from 2012, partly 
due to the much feared inﬂationary threat proving 
illusory under this low GDP growth scenario.  
In contrast to the above, World Investment under 
Scenario B continues to rise throughout the forecast, as 
the bull market for gold persists, in large measure due 
to lax monetary policy and its consequence, namely 
higher inﬂation plus the sovereign debt crisis becoming 
more severe over time.  The combination of price rises 
and increased investment tonnage means that World 
Investment in value terms in this scenario is forecast to 
reach $226 billion in 2013.  
6.2 World Investment
After a wave of long liquidation in the OTC and

has rebounded strongly, particularly from late June

expanded by over 35% in July, although a fair portion 
of this increase was driven by short covering and trend 
following purchases.  Moreover, demand for physical 
bullion products has also remained at relatively high 
levels.  Basis GFMS statistics, bar demand is estimated 
to have totalled over 500 tonnes in the ﬁrst half of 
this year, up by an impressive 35% year-on-year, with 
particularly strong growth posted in Asian markets. 
Unsurprisingly, key drivers behind this renewed investor 
interest are the worsening European sovereign debt

Portugal become the third country forced to go to the 
EU for help in May.  In addition, a year after its €110 
billion rescue, Greece came back to centre stage in 
June, as the country failed to meet the terms of its 
bailout.  Even though the latest agreement has seen 
concerns over Greek debt issue ease somewhat in the 
short term, the risks for contagion to other European 
countries will remain heightened over the next few 
months.

substantially lower in each year as the investment case 
for gold diminishes owing to falling prices.

Medals and imitation coin offtake is expected to 
undergo a double-digit decline this year in volume 
terms, but to maintain a positive trend in value 
terms.  While this signals constraints in stretching 
the expenditure required to consume higher volumes, 
at the same time it also suggests strong price 
expectations amongst small investors.  Offtake then 
suffers a material set back in the ﬁnal two years under 
the Base Case, as the start of a secular drop in prices 
hits investor conﬁdence in gold.  Unlike bar investment,

in value terms the decline remains relatively limited.

Following the heavy losses realised in 2009, world 
jewellery consumption partially recovered last year, 
rising by 11%.  This was impressive given that it 
occurred in tandem with rising and often record gold 
prices (in both dollar and local currency terms).  
However, it would be wrong to interpret this as meaning 
that the jewellery sector has lost its price sensitivity; 
India accounted for the bulk of the gains and this was 
mainly due to strong anticipatory buying and a bullish 
price outlook.  Elsewhere, demand was little changed in 
2010, which suggests that the beneﬁts of an improving 
global economy were broadly offset by ﬁrmer prices.
Under the Base Case, we are expecting a modest lift 
in jewellery offtake this year, despite gold’s anticipated 
price rise.  The year has begun in a fairly robust way 
and, although that was partly due to the ﬁrst quarter 
price retreat, strong emerging market GDP growth and 
bullish price expectations meant these gains extended 
into the second quarter.  That said, second half 
weakness, resulting largely from ﬁrmer prices (together 
with the prospects for an economic slowdown) will 
result in a far smaller gain for the full calendar year.  
In 2012, demand is expected to edge only fractionally 
lower, reﬂecting the lift to the forecast, basis annual 
average prices.  Much of this is due to the evaporation 
of anticipatory buying as price expectations become 
more bearish in many key markets.  We doubt this 
would, however, turn into a rout as an improvement in 
the affordability of jewellery will help to sustain levels.  
It is only in 2013 that falling prices contribute to a 6% 
rise in demand.
It is of note that the above forecast of broad stability in

value of consumption falls in 2013.  That this occurs 
despite ongoing global GDP growth is largely due to 
depressed speciﬁcally investment-targeted purchases.  
This stagnation in value terms is largely due to the 
marked retreat in volume terms that we are expecting 
for India, with its consumption in 2013 perhaps as 
much as 140 tonnes down on this year.  Some of these 
losses, however, should be countered by gains in China, 
although the value of these sales should also fall back 
in 2013 as the investment case behind gold begins 
to wither.  By way of contrast and again illustrating 
the importance of the investment motive, volumes in

essentially all adornment focused, should actually grow

moderately higher offtake during 2012-13.

Although the volume of jewellery demand is expected 
to improve during 2012-13, the extent of the lift will 
be relatively modest, leaving the 2013 total someway 
short of 2009’s depressed outcome.  Along with 
subdued economic growth, industrialised world retailers 
are unlikely to rush to substitute back in favour of gold, 
instead taking the opportunity, offered by weaker gold 
prices, to beneﬁt from ﬁrmer retail margins.
7.3  Developing World
Last year saw a sharp recovery in developing world gold 
jewellery consumption, which wiped out the bulk of the 
losses suffered in 2009.  However, this outcome owed 
a great deal to a much improved Indian market which, 
if excluded from this analysis, reveals that developing 
world demand was little changed in 2010, highlighting 
the adverse impact of higher gold prices (which offset 
the beneﬁts of ﬁrmer economic growth).
Looking ahead, elevated Base Case gold prices will 
negatively impact developing world jewellery demand.  
The weaker price trend in 2013 offers the prospect for 
the release of some pent-up demand, although with 
prices remaining above $1,300, the extent to which 
this occurs should be modest.  In terms of Scenario B, 
a small uplift in 2011 gives way to an uninterrupted 
period of losses through to 2013, with the potential for 
jewellery demand in 2013 to fall considerably short of 
2009’s historically low total.  In spite of the stronger 
economic growth trend, a combination of record prices 
and often high volatility will continue to dampen 
developing world jewellery demand.  In contrast, an 
improved performance under Scenario C should see 
the developing world total recover, with the 2013 total 
expected to rise to its highest point since 2001.
